Keep app alive on your device
Aggressive battery optimization on some devices (like Xiaomi, Huawei, Oppo, Vivo) may kill background services. Follow these steps to ensure Gesture Volume runs reliably:
1. Enable Auto-start: Go to Settings → Apps → Manage Apps → Gesture Volume → Enable Auto-start.
2. Battery Optimization: Set Battery Saver to \"No Restrictions\".
3. Lock in Recents: Open the \"Recent Apps\" screen, long-press the app card, and click the Lock icon 🔒.
4. Permissions: Ensure \"Display pop-up windows while running in the background\" is enabled.
For device-specific instructions, please visit dontkillmyapp.com

This is your handler at its real size. Long press the live bar on your home screen to move it.
Where is the bar? I do not see it.

It is hidden while this app is open, so it never covers its own settings. Press home and it comes back. If it is still missing, check that the service is on — the big switch at the top of the home screen — and that the Permissions card is not asking for anything.
How do I move the bar?

Press and hold it, wait for the buzz, then drag. It goes anywhere on the screen, and where you leave it is remembered separately for portrait and landscape. Which side it starts on can also be set under Appearance › Position.
How do I get rid of the bar temporarily?

Long press it and choose Hide handler. It stays away until you bring it back — from the notification, or from the card that appears on this app\'s home screen. Turning the service off entirely is the switch at the top of that screen.
The bar keeps disappearing on its own.

Your phone is stopping the app in the background. This is common on Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, Realme, Huawei and some Samsung devices, and it is not something an app can fix from the inside — battery optimisation has to be turned off for this app, and on some phones it also needs to be allowed to auto-start. Troubleshoot checks both and takes you to the right screen for your device.
Why can I change the volume but not the brightness?

Brightness needs the “Modify system settings” permission, which Android keeps separate from everything else. Grant it from the Permissions card. The app also turns adaptive brightness off the first time it writes a brightness value, because the light sensor would otherwise overwrite whatever you set within a second or two.
Why does it ask for the accessibility service?

Only for the actions Android will not let an ordinary app perform: Back, Home, Recents, screenshot, lock screen, the notification shade and the power menu. Nothing else needs it, and the picker marks those actions so you know before you choose one. It can also draw the bar without a notification — see the next question.
Can I get rid of the ongoing notification?

Yes. Turn on “Run without a notification” in Actions. The bar is then drawn by the accessibility service instead of a foreground service, and Android no longer requires a permanent notification. It also tends to survive aggressive battery managers better.

A track that grows out of the bar for setting brightness or volume. Swipe the bar up or down and it opens beside it, and the same swipe keeps setting the value. It stays on screen afterwards, so you can touch the track to correct an overshoot, and it closes itself once you are done. What it adjusts is set in Quick slider.

A panel that slides out beside the bar with your apps, shortcuts and small tools — search, a timer, a calculator, notes, the clipboard and media controls. Swipe the bar inward to open it, or assign “Open deck” to any other gesture.
What is the difference between the Quick panel and the Deck?

The Quick panel is one slider for one value. The Deck is a whole panel of shortcuts and tools. They open on different gestures — up or down for the panel, inward for the Deck — so they cannot be confused with each other.
How do I change what a tap or a swipe does?

Actions. There are six slots — single tap, double tap, triple tap, long press, swipe in and swipe out — plus the two vertical swipes, and around forty actions to put in them. A slot set to None does nothing, which also makes the gestures around it quicker: a single tap fires immediately when nothing is bound to a double tap.

Holding the bar offers a small menu of actions as well as picking the bar up to move it — hold still for the menu, move to drag. You choose what is in it, what order it is in, and whether it is a grid or a list, from Long-press menu.

By default the bar follows whatever is playing — media, a call, an alarm or the ringer — which is usually what you want but can surprise you when nothing is playing. Actions › Volume stream lets you pin it to one specific stream instead.
Yes, and the bar remembers a separate position for each orientation, so it can sit somewhere sensible in both.

Very little. The bar is a small window that draws nothing until you touch it, and the app does no work in the background between gestures. Turning off battery optimisation, which Troubleshoot suggests, does not make it use more power — it only stops the system killing it.
The bar gets in the way in games and full-screen video.

Move it somewhere the app you are using does not need — long press and drag — or make it smaller and more transparent under Appearance. The Ghost preset is close to invisible while still being there. For a game you play often, hiding the bar from the long-press menu and bringing it back from the notification afterwards is the cleanest option.

GestureVolume uses the accessibility service to perform the system actions you assign to the floating bar — lock the screen, take a screenshot, go Back or Home, open recent apps, the notification shade, quick settings and the power menu. If you choose, it also draws the bar without a persistent notification, saves text you copy into the app’s clipboard history, and opens the Quick panel the moment you press a volume key, looking at the two volume keys only. It reads nothing else, collects nothing, and everything stays on this device.
Optional: performs Lock screen, Screenshot, Back, Home, Recent apps, Notifications, Quick settings and Power menu, and can draw the bar without a notification.

GestureVolume uses Android’s accessibility service for four things, all optional:

• To perform the system actions you assign to the bar: Lock screen, Screenshot, Back, Home, Recent apps, Notifications, Quick settings and the Power menu.

• To draw the bar without a persistent notification, if you switch that on.

• To save text you copy into the clipboard history, only if you switch that on.

• To open the Quick panel the moment you press a volume key, only if you set the volume keys to Instant. It looks at the two volume keys and passes every other key straight on.

It does not read or collect anything else. Nothing leaves your device. You can turn it off at any time in Settings › Accessibility.
